{{Short description|Sensory evaluation tool}}
The '''hedonic scale''' is a [[sensory evaluation]] tool used to measure the degree of pleasure or liking of a product or service. The scale usually consists of 9 levels ranging from 1 to 9, or  "dislike extremely" to "like extremely".<ref name="Lim">{{cite journal |last1=Lim |first1=Juyun |title=Hedonic scaling: A review of methods and theory |journal=Food Quality and Preference |series=Agrostat 2010 |date=June 2011 |volume=22 |issue=8 |pages=733–747 |doi=10.1016/j.foodqual.2011.05.008 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0950329311000954 |access-date=9 September 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The hedonic scale is widely used for [[consumer acceptance testing]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Addo-Preko |first1=Emmanuel |last2=Amissah |first2=Joris Gerald Niilante |last3=Adjei |first3=Maame Yaakwaah Blay |title=The relevance of the number of categories in the hedonic scale to the Ghanaian consumer in acceptance testing |journal=Frontiers in Food Science and Technology |date=21 June 2023 |volume=3 |doi=10.3389/frfst.2023.1071216|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Hare">{{cite journal |last1=Hare |first1=Lynne B |title=Statistics Spotlight: Caveat Emptor Measuring the effectiveness of a product or process requires proper test design and data analysis |journal=Quality Progress |date=August 2024 |volume=57 |issue=8 |pages=46–49 |url=https://asq.org/quality-progress/articles/statistics-spotlight-caveat-emptor?id=2edd7a2fd7b8445ea029a08aeb4fcf22 |access-date=9 September 2024}}</ref>

== Overview ==
The main characteristics of the scale are that each category is associated with a verbal descriptor from “Dislike extremely” to “Like extremely” and that the scale has a neutral category''',''' “Neither Like nor Dislike”.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Torrico |first1=Damir Dennis |last2=Hutchings |first2=Scott C. |last3=Ha |first3=Minh |last4=Bittner |first4=Evan P. |last5=Fuentes |first5=Sigfredo |last6=Warner |first6=Robyn D. |last7=Dunshea |first7=Frank R. |date=October 2018 |title=Novel techniques to understand consumer responses towards food products: A review with a focus on meat |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0309174018302432 |journal=Meat Science |language=en |volume=144 |pages=30–42 |doi=10.1016/j.meatsci.2018.06.006|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The scale offers a chance for respondents to give extreme end answers and express their strong positive or negative feelings, such as "Dislike extremely" (1). The bipolar nature of the scale and the assumption of equal psychological distance between successive scale points make it a useful tool for some researchers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lim |first=Juyun |date=June 2011 |title=Hedonic scaling: A review of methods and theory |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0950329311000954 |journal=Food Quality and Preference |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.foodqual.2011.05.008|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== History and Development ==
The hedonic scale originated from the study of hedonic emotions, meaning subjective experiences of pleasure and displeasure. Coming from the Greek word ''[[Hedone|hēdonē]],'' meaning “pleasure”, it was designed to understand individuals’ responses to a specific stimulus. The scale is based on the roots of [[psychophysics]] and [[affective science]], which attempt to understand how to quantify emotional human responses to physical stimuli.

The 9-point hedonic scale was created by Peryam and Pilgrim in the 1950s, initially to measure food preferences amongst soldiers in the [[United States Armed Forces|U.S. Armed Forces]]. The developers applied the graphic rating scale,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nicolas |first1=Laura |last2=Marquilly |first2=Coline |last3=O’Mahony |first3=Michael |date=December 2010 |title=The 9-point hedonic scale: Are words and numbers compatible? |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0950329310001035 |journal=Food Quality and Preference |language=en |volume=21 |issue=8 |pages=1008–1015 |doi=10.1016/j.foodqual.2010.05.017|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which [[Experimental psychology|experimental psychologists]] used to measure various [[Phenomenology (psychology)|psychological phenomena]], for this case measuring the “hedonic” value of foods.

=== Current Use ===
Since then, it has adapted to the modern [[food industry]] to assess consumer acceptance and the sensory quality of food.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Society of Sensory Professionals |url=https://www.sensorysociety.org/knowledge/sspwiki/Pages/The%209-point%20Hedonic%20Scale.aspx |access-date=2025-04-21 |website=Society of Sensory Professionals |language=en-US}}</ref> Furthermore, it has become the most widely used scale in research studying hedonic perception.

== Hedonic Scale Adapted For Children ==
A number of hedonic scales for children have been proposed, some using pictures (often faces), some using words, and some a combination of pictures and words.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Popper |first1=R. |chapter=Consumer testing of food products using children |date=2007 |title=Consumer-Led Food Product Development |pages=383–406 |chapter-url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/B978184569072450016X |access-date=2025-04-21 |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1533/9781845693381.3.383 |isbn=978-1-84569-072-4 |last2=Kroll |first2=J.J.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> These newly proposed scales were adapted to suit children’s language, for example, as illustrated in the table below, replacing terms such as “extremely like” with “super good”.

Rather than using numbers to show the value of a product, the children’s hedonic scale includes different faces with various [[facial expression]]s, e.g., a smiling face suggesting “happiness”. However, these faces may unintentionally create bias or confusion. For example, children may choose the ‘happy’ face because they prefer the image itself, rather than because it represents their opinion about the food they tasted.

Other researchers highlight that the eyes and the mouth are particularly important to the interpretation of the facial expression,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Calvo |first1=Manuel G. |last2=Fernández-Martín |first2=Andrés |last3=Nummenmaa |first3=Lauri |date=June 2013 |title=A smile biases the recognition of eye expressions: Configural projection from a salient mouth |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1080/17470218.2012.732586 |journal=Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology |language=en |volume=66 |issue=6 |pages=1159–1181 |doi=10.1080/17470218.2012.732586 |pmid=23140405 |issn=1747-0218|url-access=subscription }}</ref> making the design of the children’s version of the hedonic scale especially crucial to its effectiveness.

== Cultural Considerations ==
Despite its widespread use, the hedonic scale may not be applicable due to cultural and [[Linguistics|linguistic]] differences. This can affect the respondents’ interpretations of the scale, specifically when it comes to translating them, as some terms will not have the same meaning when translated. For instance, Spanish-speaking participants may interpret “extremely” differently, potentially skewing responses.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Curia |first1=Ana Valeria |last2=Hough |first2=Guillermo |last3=Martı́nez |first3=Marı́a Carolina |last4=Margalef |first4=Marı́a Isabel |date=April 2004 |title=How Argentine consumers understand the Spanish translation of the 9-point hedonic scale |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S095032930100012X |journal=Food Quality and Preference |language=en |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=217–221 |doi=10.1016/S0950-3293(01)00012-X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Similarly, in many Asian cultures, respondents tend to avoid extreme responses to maintain harmony.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Chuansheng |last2=Lee |first2=Shin-ying |last3=Stevenson |first3=Harold W. |date=May 1995 |title=Response Style and Cross-Cultural Comparisons of Rating Scales Among East Asian and North American Students |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1995.tb00327.x |journal=Psychological Science |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=170–175 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9280.1995.tb00327.x |issn=0956-7976|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This can result in [[Cluster analysis|data clustering]] around the midpoint, reducing the sensitivity of the scale.

The interpretation and understanding of the facial expression used for the children’s hedonic scale is not [[Universalism|universal]] across different cultures. For example, a smiling face may not convey the same emotion amongst different societies, highlighting the importance of adapting each hedonic scale to the culture of the country it’s being used in to ensure accurate results.

== Advantages ==

=== Simple to understand ===
The scale is easy and quick to complete, which makes it suitable for people of all ages and different [[literacy]] levels. Due to its simplicity, it increases the likelihood of people responding to the scale and taking part in research.

=== Ability to Quantify Responses ===
The scale can turn emotions and preferences, such as liking or disliking stimuli, into numerical values. This enables researchers to perform calculations and [[Statistical inference|statistical analysis]] of personal preferences, increasing the objectivity and [[Reliability (statistics)|reliability]] of the research.

=== Real-world application ===
The scale is widely used within the food industry for practical reasons, such as planning of menus; for example, items that receive low reviews can be removed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wichchukit |first1=Sukanya |last2=O'Mahony |first2=Michael |date=2015-08-30 |title=The 9-point hedonic scale and hedonic ranking in food science: some reappraisals and alternatives |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jsfa.6993 |journal=Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture |language=en |volume=95 |issue=11 |pages=2167–2178 |doi=10.1002/jsfa.6993 |pmid=25378223 |bibcode=2015JSFA...95.2167W |issn=0022-5142|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This may contribute to [[Customer satisfaction|consumer satisfaction]] by improving the quality and appeal of available products, therefore increasing [[Utility|overall utility]].

=== High face validity ===
The scale asks respondents how much they like or dislike a stimulus with clear and familiar language.  This means that participants easily understand what the scale measures, hence increasing the authenticity of the responses.

== Disadvantages ==

=== Suffers from beta cultural bias ===
The scale does not translate accurately into Spanish<ref name=":0" /> and other Asian languages,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yeh |first1=L.L |last2=Kim |first2=K.O |last3=Chompreeda |first3=P |last4=Rimkeeree |first4=H |last5=Yau |first5=N.J.N |last6=Lundahl |first6=D.S |date=November 1998 |title=Comparison in Use of the 9-Point Hedonic Scale between Americans, Chinese, Koreans, and Thai |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0950329398000287 |journal=Food Quality and Preference |language=en |volume=9 |issue=6 |pages=413–419 |doi=10.1016/S0950-3293(98)00028-7|url-access=subscription }}</ref> demonstrating it lacks generalisability across cultures. The most reported complaint is the different meaning of the word “extreme” in these languages.

=== Challenging to analyse ===
The scale produces [[ordinal data]], but it is treated as [[Level of measurement|interval data]] for statistical analyses like [[Analysis of variance|ANOVA]]. This mismatch can make data analysis challenging, as it assumes equal spacing between response options when this may not be the case. As a result, it may lead to inaccurate conclusions and reduce the overall reliability and [[Validity (statistics)|validity]] of the research findings.

=== Chance of response bias ===
The scale includes a neutral midpoint, which can result in a central tendency error, where respondents avoid using extreme ends and they don't express their real opinions. This can result in non-representative data and reduce the [[external validity]] of findings.

=== Absence of qualitative insights ===
The scale measures overall liking or disliking; however, it doesn’t reveal the specific reasons behind those responses. As a result, it struggles to understand why respondents feel a certain way, which can limit the practical element of the scale.
